pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Ceredigion, Wales, founded 1164 as a daughter of Whitland; the vale of flowers, burial place of Welsh princes)
etymology: Latin strata florida, the flowery way or vale of flowers, rendering the Welsh Ystrad Fflur, the meadow of the stream Fflur.
biblical_def: Strata Florida, in Welsh Ystrad Fflur, was founded in 1164 in the uplands of Ceredigion, a daughter of Whitland, and became the chief house of the Welsh Cistercians and the burial place of princes of the house of Dyfed and Deheubarth. The poet Dafydd ap Gwilym is traditionally buried there under a yew. Of the great church only a magnificent carved west doorway and the floor plan remain. An abbey built as a princely mausoleum is the entry's subject, and the Psalter has a flat refusal to be impressed by princes: “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psa 146:3), and the reason in the next verse — “His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish” (Psa 146:4). The name invites the other text. “But the rich, in that he is made low: because as the flower of the grass he shall pass away” (Jam 1:10), and “so also shall the rich man fade away in his ways” (Jam 1:11). A vale of flowers full of princes' tombs makes James's point without help.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines prince as a sovereign, a chief ruler, and also the son of a king; mausoleum as a magnificent tomb or stately sepulchral monument; and flower as the delicate and gaily colored petals of a plant, and figuratively the prime or choicest part.
webster_full: PRINCE, n. In a general sense, a sovereign; the chief and independent ruler of a nation or state; also, the son of a king or emperor.
MAUSOLEUM, n. A magnificent tomb, or stately sepulchral monument.
SEPULCHRE, n. A grave; a tomb; a place where a dead body is interred, or a place destined for that purpose.
FLOWER, n. The delicate and gaily colored leaves or petals of a plant; figuratively, the prime, the choicest part.
MEADOW, n. A tract of low land, appropriated to the culture of grass for hay.
scriptures: Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help.
His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish.
Jam 1:10
But the rich, in that he is made low: because as the flower of the grass he shall pass away.
Jam 1:11

For the sun is no sooner risen with a burning heat, but it withereth the grass, and the flower thereof falleth, and the grace of the fashion of it perisheth: so also shall the rich man fade away in his ways.
corruption_summary: The chief Welsh Cistercian house, the vale of flowers, built as a burial place for princes: a name and a purpose that argue against each other.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the abbey as mausoleum — a house of prayer whose chief business became the commemoration of the great. Masses for the dead were the economic engine of the later Middle Ages, and a princely burial bought perpetual intercession. Scripture allows none of it, for the same reason it allows no trust in princes: “There is no man that hath power over the spirit to retain the spirit; neither hath he power in the day of death: and there is no discharge in that war” (Ecc 8:8).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the levelling realism of “in that very day his thoughts perish” (Psa 146:4). The nationalist use of Strata Florida — a shrine of Welsh identity — is a gentler modern version of the same instinct, and the abbey's own name keeps answering it: the flower of the grass passes away.
roots_summary: Latin strata florida, flowery way; Welsh Ystrad Fflur; Hebrew nadib (H5081), a noble; Greek anthos (G438), a flower; Hebrew ruach (H7307), breath or spirit.
roots_lines: Latin strata florida — the flowery way; the Latin form of the Welsh Ystrad Fflur.
Hebrew nadib (H5081) — a noble, a prince; “Put not your trust in princes” (Psa 146:3).
Hebrew ruach (H7307) — breath, wind, spirit; “His breath goeth forth” (Psa 146:4).
Greek anthos (G438) — a flower; “as the flower of the grass he shall pass away” (Jam 1:10).
Greek chortos (G5528) — grass, herbage; “but it withereth the grass” (Jam 1:11).
usage: “nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psa 146:3) — said over a house full of princes.
“and the grace of the fashion of it perisheth” (Jam 1:11) — the vale of flowers, read theologically.
“neither hath he power in the day of death” (Ecc 8:8) — the answer to purchased intercession.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey near Llangollen in north Wales, founded 1201; the valley of the cross)
etymology: Latin vallis crucis, the valley of the cross; named from the Pillar of Eliseg, a ninth-century stone cross standing near the site.
biblical_def: Valle Crucis was founded in 1201 in the Dee valley near Llangollen, a daughter of Strata Marcella, and takes its name from the stone cross that already stood there — the Pillar of Eliseg, a ninth-century memorial raised by a prince of Powys. Its church and east range survive substantially, among the best-preserved monastic buildings in Wales. The name is the best in this dictionary and deserves to be taken at full weight, because the cross is the centre of the faith and not a landscape feature. “For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God” (1Co 1:18) makes it a message and a power; “Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross” (Col 2:14) states what was accomplished there; and “he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phi 2:8) names the obedience. A valley named for a cross has the whole gospel in its address, and nothing in the monastic system could add to it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cross as a gibbet consisting of two pieces of timber placed across each other, and figuratively the sufferings of Christ and the doctrine of the atonement; and crucify as to nail to a cross, to put to death by nailing the hands and feet to a cross.
webster_full: CROSS, n. A gibbet consisting of two pieces of timber placed across each other, either in form of a T or of an X.
CROSS, n. The instrument of Christ's crucifixion; hence, the sufferings of Christ; also, the doctrine of Christ's sufferings and of the atonement.
CRUCIFY, v.t. To nail to a cross; to put to death by nailing the hands and feet to a cross or gibbet.
ATONEMENT, n. Expiation; satisfaction or reparation made by giving an equivalent for an injury, or by doing or suffering that which is received in satisfaction for an offense.
PILLAR, n. A kind of irregular column, round and insulated; a supporter; that which sustains or upholds.
scriptures: For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God.
Col 2:14
Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross;
Phi 2:8
And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
Gal 6:14
But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world.
corruption_summary: A north Welsh abbey named for a ninth-century stone cross: the best name in this dictionary, and a gospel nothing monastic could add to.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the cross made an object rather than a message — carved, carried, kissed, multiplied in relics of the True Cross until, as Calvin dryly noted, there was timber enough for a ship. Paul will not have the cross as an artefact; he has it as a proclamation and a boast: “But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world” (Gal 6:14).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the offence of the thing. “the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness” (1Co 1:18) says the message will sound absurd, and a Christianity that never sounds absurd to anyone has probably stopped preaching the cross and started preaching the valley it stands in.
roots_summary: Latin vallis crucis, valley of the cross; Greek stauros (G4716), a cross; Greek stauroo (G4717), to crucify; Hebrew ets (H6086), a tree; Greek cheirographon (G5498), a handwriting or bond.
roots_lines: Latin vallis crucis — the valley of the cross; the abbey's name from the Pillar of Eliseg.
Greek stauros (G4716) — an upright stake, a cross; “For the preaching of the cross” (1Co 1:18).
Greek stauroo (G4717) — to crucify; “by whom the world is crucified unto me” (Gal 6:14).
Greek cheirographon (G5498) — a handwritten bond; “Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us” (Col 2:14).
Hebrew ets (H6086) — a tree, timber; the Old Testament word the apostles apply to the cross.
usage: “nailing it to his cross” (Col 2:14) — what was done there, stated in a clause.
“even the death of the cross” (Phi 2:8) — the depth of the obedience.
“save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal 6:14) — the only permitted boast.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in north Wales, founded about 1186 and moved to Maenan in 1283 when Edward I took its site for Conwy Castle)
etymology: Welsh aber, a river mouth, with the river Conwy: the mouth of the Conwy.
biblical_def: Aberconwy was founded about 1186 at the mouth of the Conwy, a daughter of Strata Florida, and became the favoured house of Llywelyn the Great, who was buried there. In 1283, having conquered Gwynedd, Edward I decided to build his castle and walled town on the abbey's site; the monks were moved upriver to Maenan and compensated, and Conwy Castle stands where their church stood. A monastery displaced so that a fortress of conquest might occupy its ground is an unusually literal case, and the prophets have the words for it. “Woe to him that buildeth a town with blood, and stablisheth a city by iniquity!” (Hab 2:12); and Micah of the rulers of Jerusalem, “They build up Zion with blood, and Jerusalem with iniquity” (Mic 3:10). The qualification over all such building is the psalm the Cistercians knew by heart: “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain” (Psa 127:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conquest as the act of conquering, the subjection of a country by force; castle as a house fortified for defense against an enemy; and iniquity as injustice, unrighteousness, a sin or crime.
webster_full: CONQUEST, n. The act of conquering; the subjection of a country or people by arms; also, that which is conquered; possession gained by force.
CASTLE, n. A house fortified for defense against an enemy; a fortress; the mansion of a nobleman or prince.
INIQUITY, n. Injustice; unrighteousness; a deviation from rectitude; also, a particular deviation from rectitude; a sin or crime.
ABER, n. In the Celtic languages, the mouth of a river, or the confluence of waters; used in many names of places.
DISPLACE, v.t. To put out of the usual or proper place; to remove from its place; to disorder.
scriptures: Hab 2:12
Woe to him that buildeth a town with blood, and stablisheth a city by iniquity!
Mic 3:10
They build up Zion with blood, and Jerusalem with iniquity.
A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
Hab 2:11
For the stone shall cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it.
corruption_summary: A Welsh abbey turned out of its own ground in 1283 so that Edward I could build Conwy Castle there: Habakkuk's woe, in masonry.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is conquest wearing a lawful face. The monks were compensated and the transaction was regular; the ground was still taken by a conqueror for a fortress to hold a conquered people, and Habakkuk does not accept paperwork as an answer: “For the stone shall cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it” (Hab 2:11). The stones of Conwy are among the finest in Europe, and the prophet says what they say.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that no building, however magnificent or legal, carries a guarantee. “except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain” (Psa 127:1) is addressed to builders of cities and walls, and Conwy's walls are still there while the kingdom that raised them is not.
roots_summary: Welsh aber, a river mouth; Hebrew dam (H1818), blood; Hebrew avlah (H5766), iniquity; Hebrew ir (H5892), a city; Hebrew shamar (H8104), to keep or watch.
roots_lines: Welsh aber — the mouth of a river; one of the commonest elements in Welsh place names.
Hebrew dam (H1818) — blood; “Woe to him that buildeth a town with blood” (Hab 2:12).
Hebrew avlah (H5766) — injustice, iniquity; “and Jerusalem with iniquity” (Mic 3:10).
Hebrew ir (H5892) — a city; “except the LORD keep the city” (Psa 127:1).
Hebrew shamar (H8104) — to keep, guard, watch; the watchman's vain vigil.
usage: “and stablisheth a city by iniquity!” (Hab 2:12) — the woe over a fortress of conquest.
“For the stone shall cry out of the wall” (Hab 2:11) — what good masonry says when it is ill-got.
“they labour in vain that build it” (Psa 127:1) — over abbey and castle alike.

pos: n. (an abbey in Flintshire, Savigniac from 1131 and Cistercian from 1147, beside the pilgrimage well at Holywell)
etymology: Old English personal name with weorc, a fortification: the stronghold of Basing's people, from an earlier earthwork on the site.
biblical_def: Basingwerk stands on the Dee estuary in Flintshire, founded in 1131 as a house of Savigny and absorbed into the Cistercian order in 1147. Its great asset was not land but a spring: the abbey held the shrine of St Winefride's Well at Holywell a mile away, one of the busiest pilgrimage sites in Britain, and drew income from the pilgrims who came to bathe for healing. The practice is old and the biblical case against it is not a sneer but an argument. Naaman wanted a river and a ritual and was given a command instead: “Are not Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? may I not wash in them, and be clean? So he turned and went away in a rage” (2Ki 5:12), and his servant's rebuke is the point — “if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing, wouldest thou not have done it? how much rather then, when he saith to thee, Wash, and be clean?” (2Ki 5:13). Healing came by obedience to a word, not by the virtue of a water.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines well as a spring, a fountain, also a pit sunk into the earth to the water; pilgrimage as a journey to some place deemed sacred and venerable, in order to pay devotion to the relics of a saint; and shrine as a case, box or receptacle for sacred things.
webster_full: WELL, n. A spring; a fountain; also, a pit or cylindrical hole, sunk perpendicularly into the earth to the water.
PILGRIMAGE, n. A long journey, particularly a journey to some place deemed sacred and venerable, in order to pay devotion to the relics of some deceased saint.
SHRINE, n. A case, box or receptacle for holy things; particularly, a case in which the relics of a saint are deposited.
HEALING, a. Tending to cure; mild; mollifying; also, the act of curing or restoring to soundness.
HOLY WELL, a spring or well held in veneration, and resorted to for the supposed virtue of its waters.
scriptures: Are not Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? may I not wash in them, and be clean? So he turned and went away in a rage.

And his servants came near, and spake unto him, and said, My father, if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing, wouldest thou not have done it? how much rather then, when he saith to thee, Wash, and be clean?
Joh 4:14
But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.
Joh 5:7
The impotent man answered him, Sir, I have no man, when the water is troubled, to put me into the pool: but while I am coming, another steppeth down before me.
corruption_summary: A Flintshire abbey whose income came from a pilgrimage well: healing sought from a water, where Scripture gives it by obedience to a word.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the holy well, and Scripture answers it in two places. Naaman's story shows the appetite for a ritual with a famous water in it, and shows God refusing to indulge it. And the pool of Bethesda is the clearest case of all: the man had waited beside healing water for years and got nothing from it — “Sir, I have no man, when the water is troubled, to put me into the pool: but while I am coming, another steppeth down before me” (Joh 5:7) — and Christ healed him with a sentence, standing beside the pool and not using it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one water Scripture does commend, which is a person: “but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life” (Joh 4:14). A well is a good figure and a poor shrine.
roots_summary: Old English weorc, a fortification; Hebrew rachats (H7364), to wash; Hebrew taher (H2891), to be clean; Greek kolumbethra (G2861), a pool; Greek pege (G4077), a spring.
roots_lines: Old English weorc — a work, a fortification; the abbey built on an older earthwork.
Hebrew rachats (H7364) — to wash, bathe; “Wash, and be clean?” (2Ki 5:13).
Hebrew taher (H2891) — to be clean, pure; the condition Naaman wanted and got by obeying.
Greek kolumbethra (G2861) — a pool for bathing; “to put me into the pool” (Joh 5:7).
Greek pege (G4077) — a spring; “a well of water springing up into everlasting life” (Joh 4:14).
usage: “So he turned and went away in a rage” (2Ki 5:12) — the appetite for a famous water, thwarted.
“if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing” (2Ki 5:13) — the servant's rebuke to it.
“another steppeth down before me” (Joh 5:7) — years beside healing water and nothing gained.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Glamorgan, founded 1147 as a daughter of Clairvaux; its nave serves as the parish church)
etymology: From the Welsh locality; a place name of uncertain derivation, recorded long before the abbey.
biblical_def: Margam was founded in 1147 in Glamorgan by Robert of Gloucester, a daughter of Clairvaux and one of the wealthiest Welsh houses, with granges along the coastal plain. Its twelve-sided chapter house, now roofless, is the finest in Wales, and its nave — like that at Holm Cultram — survives as the parish church, so that a Cistercian building has housed a Welsh congregation continuously for nearly nine centuries. The abbey also kept a chronicle that is a principal source for Welsh history. This dictionary has said repeatedly that the holiness was never in the stone, and that is true; it has also said that a lament over an empty church is permitted. Margam allows the third and happiest case: a building that is simply still in use. “Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ” (1Pe 2:5) is the real construction, and “that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD” (Psa 27:4) is a desire a plain parish church can serve as well as a cathedral.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines chapter house as the house where a chapter meets; nave as the middle or body of a church; and beauty as that assemblage of graces, or an assemblage of properties, which pleases the eye.
webster_full: CHAPTER-HOUSE, n. A house or apartment where a chapter meets for the transaction of business.
NAVE, n. The middle or body of a church, extending from the balustrade of the choir to the chief entrance.
BEAUTY, n. An assemblage of graces, or an assemblage of properties in the form of a person or of any other object, which pleases the eye.
CONTINUANCE, n. A holding on or remaining in a particular state; perseverance; duration; a remaining in the same state.
GRANGE, n. A farm, with the buildings, stables, etc.; a farm house with the adjoining buildings.
scriptures: Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ.
Psa 27:4
One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple.
And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it.
Psa 26:8
LORD, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thine honour dwelleth.
corruption_summary: A wealthy Glamorgan house of 1147 whose nave has served a Welsh congregation for nine centuries: the happiest of the fates in this dictionary, a building still in use.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the prayer of “And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it” (Psa 90:17) — a request for beauty to rest on people and for their work to be made to last, which is the right order of the two.

The live caution is wealth, which was Margam's condition and the usual Cistercian trajectory. A house with granges down a whole coastal plain had already travelled a long way from Cîteaux, and the honest note to end on is that its parish church survives because ordinary people needed it, not because its abbots were careful: “LORD, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thine honour dwelleth” (Psa 26:8).
roots_summary: Hebrew noam (H5278), beauty or pleasantness; Hebrew bayith (H1004), a house; Greek lithos (G3037), a stone; Greek oikos pneumatikos, a spiritual house; Hebrew kabod (H3519), glory or honour.
roots_lines: Hebrew noam (H5278) — pleasantness, beauty; “let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us” (Psa 90:17).
Hebrew bayith (H1004) — a house; the word of both temple and household.
Hebrew kabod (H3519) — weight, glory, honour; “the place where thine honour dwelleth” (Psa 26:8).
Greek lithos (G3037) — a stone; “as lively stones” (1Pe 2:5).
Greek pneumatikos (G4152) — spiritual; the kind of house and sacrifice Peter has in view.
usage: “One thing have I desired of the LORD” (Psa 27:4) — a desire a parish church can serve.
“to offer up spiritual sacrifices” (1Pe 2:5) — the building that actually matters.
“the work of our hands establish thou it” (Psa 90:17) — the only way anything lasts.

pos: n. (an abbey in Glamorgan, Savigniac from 1130 and Cistercian from 1147; called by Leland the fairest abbey in all Wales)
etymology: From the river Nedd, Welsh Nedd, perhaps a word for shining or glistening water; the English form is Neath.
biblical_def: Neath was founded in 1130 on the river Nedd in Glamorgan as a house of Savigny, joining the Cistercians with the rest of that congregation in 1147. It became large and handsome, and the Tudor antiquary John Leland, who saw it not long before the dissolution, called it the fairest abbey in all Wales. The ruins are extensive and stand beside industrial works, which is itself a Welsh parable. Beauty in a church is the question the entry raises, and Scripture's answer is not the Cistercian one. The order's early statutes forbade sculpture, coloured glass and towers, on the ground that ornament distracts; Scripture nowhere says so, and the tabernacle and temple were made deliberately beautiful by God's own instruction. What Scripture insists is that the beauty to be sought is God's: “to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple” (Psa 27:4), and “And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us” (Psa 90:17). A fair building is permitted; a fair building admired instead of God is the fault.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fair as handsome, beautiful, pleasing to the eye; ornament as that which embellishes, something which adorns; and glory as brightness, lustre, splendor, and the divine presence.
webster_full: FAIR, a. Handsome; beautiful; properly, having a beautiful form and color; pleasing to the eye.
ORNAMENT, n. That which embellishes; something which, added to another thing, renders it more beautiful to the eye.
GLORY, n. Brightness; lustre; splendor; also, honor; praise; fame; and in scripture, the divine presence or the manifestation of the divine perfections.
ADORN, v.t. To deck or dress with ornaments; to embellish; to set off to advantage.
PLAIN, a. Without beauty; not handsome; also, artless; simple; not ostentatious.
scriptures: Psa 27:4
One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple.
And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it.
Exo 28:2
And thou shalt make holy garments for Aaron thy brother for glory and for beauty.
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
corruption_summary: Called the fairest abbey in Wales: beauty in a church is permitted by Scripture and was forbidden by the order's own statutes, and the real fault is admiring it instead of God.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption has two forms and the Cistercians fell into the second. The first is ornament that swallows worship, which is a real danger. The second is the belief that plainness is itself holiness — a doctrine Scripture does not teach, since God commanded garments “And thou shalt make holy garments for Aaron thy brother for glory and for beauty” (Exo 28:2) and filled his own house with workmanship. An order that legislated against beauty had added to the law.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the order of beauties. “But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price” (1Pe 3:4) prefers an inward adornment without forbidding the outward, and “to behold the beauty of the LORD” (Psa 27:4) names the beauty worth crossing a country to see.
roots_summary: Welsh Nedd, the river name; Hebrew tiphereth (H8597), beauty or glory; Hebrew noam (H5278), pleasantness; Greek kosmos (G2889) in the sense of adornment; Greek praus (G4239), meek.
roots_lines: Welsh Nedd — the river that names the town and the abbey.
Hebrew tiphereth (H8597) — beauty, glory, ornament; “for glory and for beauty” (Exo 28:2).
Hebrew noam (H5278) — pleasantness, loveliness; “to behold the beauty of the LORD” (Psa 27:4).
Greek kosmos (G2889) — order, and so adornment; the root of English cosmetic.
Greek praus (G4239) — meek, gentle; “the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit” (1Pe 3:4).
usage: “And thou shalt make holy garments for Aaron thy brother” (Exo 28:2) — beauty commanded, not merely permitted.
“which is in the sight of God of great price” (1Pe 3:4) — the adornment that is preferred.
“let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us” (Psa 90:17) — the prayer that orders the rest.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Carmarthenshire, founded 1140 as a daughter of Clairvaux; mother of the Welsh Cistercian houses)
etymology: Latin alba landa, the white land or glade, Welsh Hendy-gwyn ar Daf, the old white house on the Taf; the English Whitland is the same name.
biblical_def: Whitland in Carmarthenshire was founded in 1140 as a daughter of Clairvaux and became the mother house of the Welsh Cistercians — Strata Florida, Strata Marcella, Cwmhir, Aberconwy and others descend from it. The Welsh houses were notable for identifying with the native princes rather than with the Anglo-Norman settlement, and Whitland's daughters kept Welsh chronicles and sheltered Welsh poetry. Almost nothing of the abbey survives. The name is the entry's subject: the white house, and white is Scripture's colour of cleansing, which it never ascribes to a habit or a wall. “Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool” (Isa 1:18); “Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Psa 51:7); and the one explanation the Bible gives of how robes get white: “These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev 7:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines white as being in the color of pure snow, snowy, and figuratively pure, clear, free from spot; land as earth, the solid matter which constitutes the fixed part of the surface of the globe; and purge as to cleanse, to clear, to purify.
webster_full: WHITE, a. Being in the color of pure snow; snowy; of the color of milk or of a fresh fallen snow.
WHITE, a. Pure; clear; free from spot; as, to make one's self white before God.
LAND, n. Earth; the solid matter which constitutes the fixed part of the surface of the globe, in distinction from water.
PURGE, v.t. To cleanse or purify by separating and carrying off whatever is impure, heterogeneous or superfluous.
CRIMSON, n. A deep red color, or red slightly tinged with blue; also, red color in general.
scriptures: Isa 1:18
Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
Psa 51:7
Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.
Rev 7:14
And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
Rev 7:9

After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands;
corruption_summary: The mother house of the Welsh Cistercians, the white house: white is Scripture's colour of cleansing, and it never comes from a habit or a wall.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is whiteness as appearance. The Cistercians were the White Monks, undyed wool against the Benedictine black, and the colour was meant to preach purity; a garment cannot confer it, and Christ's hardest word to the religious of his day was about a whiteness that was exterior only. The one laundry Scripture names is bloody and belongs to someone else: “made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev 7:14).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the offer in Isaiah, which is startling in its reasonableness: “Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD” (Isa 1:18). God proposes to argue a man out of his guilt by telling him what he will do with it, and the white robes of the redeemed are worn by a multitude from every nation: “of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne” (Rev 7:9).
roots_summary: Latin alba landa, white glade; Hebrew laban (H3835), to be white; Hebrew sheleg (H7950), snow; Greek leukos (G3022), white; Greek leukaino (G3021), to whiten.
roots_lines: Latin alba landa — the white glade; the Welsh Hendy-gwyn carries the same sense.
Hebrew laban (H3835) — to be or make white; “wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Psa 51:7).
Hebrew sheleg (H7950) — snow; “they shall be as white as snow” (Isa 1:18).
Greek leukos (G3022) — white, bright; the colour of the robes of the redeemed.
Greek leukaino (G3021) — to whiten; “and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev 7:14).
usage: “though your sins be as scarlet” (Isa 1:18) — the condition God proposes to reason about.
“have washed their robes” (Rev 7:14) — the only whitening Scripture describes.
“Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean” (Psa 51:7) — the prayer behind the colour.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey on the Tay in Fife, founded 1227 by Queen Ermengarde as a daughter of Melrose)
etymology: From Gaelic elements, probably baile, a settlement, with a personal or descriptive element; the Scots form is Balmerino or Balmerinoch.
biblical_def: Balmerino was founded in 1227 on the south shore of the Tay in Fife by Ermengarde de Beaumont, widow of William the Lion, with monks from Melrose; she was buried there. It was never large, was burnt by the English in 1547, and survives as fragments of the chapter house and undercroft beside an ancient Spanish chestnut. A royal widow's foundation is a convenient place to set out what Scripture asks of Christians in regard to rulers, which is a good deal less than patronage and a good deal more than opinion. “I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men” (1Ti 2:1) comes first; then “For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty” (1Ti 2:2). The aim named is a quiet life, not a Christian state, and the means is prayer. “For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour” (1Ti 2:3) adds that God likes it, which is more than can be said for most Christian political activity.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines queen as the consort of a king, and also a woman who is the sovereign of a kingdom; intercession as prayer or solicitation to one party in favor of another; and dowager as a widow with a dower or jointure.
webster_full: QUEEN, n. The consort of a king; also, a woman who is the sovereign of a kingdom; as Elizabeth, queen of England.
INTERCESSION, n. Mediation; interposition between parties at variance, with a view to reconciliation; prayer or solicitation to one party in favor of another.
DOWAGER, n. A widow with a dower or jointure; a title particularly given to the widows of princes and persons of rank.
SUPPLICATION, n. Entreaty; humble and earnest prayer in worship; petition.
PEACEABLE, a. Free from war, tumult or public commotion; quiet; undisturbed; not quarrelsome.
scriptures: I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men;
For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty.
For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour;
Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help.
corruption_summary: A small Fife house founded in 1227 by a king's widow: a convenient place to state that Scripture asks prayer for rulers and aims at a quiet life.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the order and the aim of “that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty” (1Ti 2:2). Paul wrote it under Nero. He asks for prayer rather than agitation and names a modest goal, and most Christian political energy in any century has been spent on neither.

The live corruption is the courting of power by the church, of which royal foundations are the medieval form and access to governments the modern one. The Psalter supplies the corrective in one line: “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psa 146:3) — which is compatible with praying for them daily, and incompatible with depending on them.
roots_summary: Gaelic baile, a settlement; Hebrew melek (H4428), a king; Greek enteuxis (G1783), intercession; Greek hesuchios (G2272), quiet; Greek eusebeia (G2150), godliness.
roots_lines: Gaelic baile — a settlement or homestead; the commonest element in Scottish place names.
Hebrew melek (H4428) — a king; the figure Scripture tells us to pray for and not to trust.
Greek enteuxis (G1783) — intercession, a petition on another's behalf; “supplications, prayers, intercessions” (1Ti 2:1).
Greek hesuchios (G2272) — quiet, tranquil; “a quiet and peaceable life” (1Ti 2:2).
Greek eusebeia (G2150) — godliness, piety; the quality the quiet life is for.
usage: “be made for all men” (1Ti 2:1) — the breadth of the prayer commanded.
“For kings, and for all that are in authority” (1Ti 2:2) — written under Nero.
“Put not your trust in princes” (Psa 146:3) — compatible with praying for them, not with leaning on them.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Galloway, founded about 1192 as a daughter of Dundrennan; its chapter house survives entire)
etymology: Gaelic gleann, a narrow valley, with the river Luce; the glen of the Luce water.
biblical_def: Glenluce was founded about 1192 in the Water of Luce valley in Galloway by Roland, lord of Galloway, a daughter of Dundrennan in the Melrose line. Its vaulted chapter house stands complete and is the best thing on the site. Glenluce sits in the oldest Christian ground in Scotland: Whithorn, a dozen miles away, was a Christian centre from the fifth century, centuries before any monastic order existed, and Galloway had churches when the Cistercians were unimagined. That matters for the argument of these entries, because the gospel in Britain is older than every institution in this dictionary. “But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth” (Act 1:8) is how it travelled; Paul's own ambition was to reach ground nobody had worked: “Yea, so have I strived to preach the gospel, not where Christ was named, lest I should build upon another man's foundation” (Rom 15:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines glen as a valley, a dale, a depression or space between hills; mission as a sending, and a station of missionaries; and foundation as the basis or lowest part of an edifice, and the act of founding.
webster_full: GLEN, n. A valley; a dale; a depression or space between hills.
MISSION, n. A sending or being sent, usually by authority, to perform some service; persons sent; a station of missionaries.
FOUNDATION, n. The basis or lowest part of an edifice, or of a wall, which sustains the rest; also, the act of founding.
WITNESS, n. Testimony; attestation of a fact or event; also, one who sees or knows, and who testifies to what he has seen or known.
UTTERMOST, a. Extreme; being in the furthest, greatest or highest degree.
scriptures: Act 1:8

But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.
Yea, so have I strived to preach the gospel, not where Christ was named, lest I should build upon another man's foundation:
And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!
Isa 52:7

How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!
corruption_summary: A Galloway house of about 1192 in the oldest Christian ground in Scotland: the gospel reached Whithorn centuries before any order existed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the priority of the gospel over the institutions that later carried it. Galloway had Christians before it had monks, and “and ye shall be witnesses unto me” (Act 1:8) describes the mechanism: ordinary witnesses, sent, with power given rather than organised.

The live corruption is institutional self-importance — a church or order that comes to believe the faith arrived with it. Paul measured himself the other way, wanting unworked ground precisely so as not to take credit for another man's labour: “lest I should build upon another man's foundation” (Rom 15:20), and the sending itself is the beautiful thing: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings” (Isa 52:7).
roots_summary: Gaelic gleann, a glen; Greek martus (G3144), a witness; Greek apostello (G649), to send out; Greek themelios (G2310), a foundation; Hebrew basar (H1319), to bear tidings.
roots_lines: Gaelic gleann — a narrow valley; the first element of hundreds of Scottish names.
Greek martus (G3144) — a witness; “and ye shall be witnesses unto me” (Act 1:8).
Greek apostello (G649) — to send forth; “And how shall they preach, except they be sent?” (Rom 10:15).
Greek themelios (G2310) — a foundation; “another man's foundation” (Rom 15:20).
Hebrew basar (H1319) — to bear good tidings; “that publisheth peace” (Isa 52:7).
usage: “unto the uttermost part of the earth” (Act 1:8) — how the gospel reached Galloway.
“not where Christ was named” (Rom 15:20) — Paul's refusal to take another's credit.
“that bringeth good tidings of good” (Isa 52:7) — the beauty of the sending itself.

pos: n. (the first Cistercian abbey in Ireland, founded 1142 by Malachy of Armagh with monks from Clairvaux; the fountain of honey)
etymology: Latin mellis fons, the fountain of honey; the Irish name An Mhainistir Mhór means simply the great monastery.
biblical_def: Mellifont, founded in 1142 on the Mattock in County Louth by Malachy of Armagh with monks Bernard sent from Clairvaux, was the first Cistercian house in Ireland and the head of its own filiation. Its octagonal lavabo, where the monks washed before meals, is the finest thing left. Its history turns on a conflict worth close attention: the Irish daughter houses, staffed by Irish monks with Irish customs, resisted the uniform discipline that French and English visitors came to impose, and in the troubles of the 1220s the order had to depose abbots and re-staff houses from abroad to force conformity. Both sides had a case, and Scripture holds the balance. There are things that must be insisted on — Paul withstood Peter to his face over one: “If thou, being a Jew, livest after the manner of Gentiles, and not as do the Jews, why compellest thou the Gentiles to live as do the Jews?” (Gal 2:14). And there are things that must not be: “Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind” (Rom 14:5) and “Who art thou that judgest another man's servant?” (Rom 14:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines uniformity as resemblance to each other, conformity to one rule or mode; conformity as correspondence in form, manner or use, agreement; and indifferent as neutral, and having no influence or preponderating weight.
webster_full: UNIFORMITY, n. Resemblance to each other; similitude between the parts of a whole; conformity to one rule or mode; consonancy.
CONFORMITY, n. Correspondence in form, manner or use; resemblance; agreement; congruity with.
INDIFFERENT, a. Neutral; not having sufficient reason to prefer one thing to another; also, impartial; unbiased.
LAVATORY, n. A place for washing; also, a wash or lotion for a diseased part.
CUSTOM, n. Frequent or common use, or practice; a frequent repetition of the same act; established manner.
scriptures: Gal 2:14

But when I saw that they walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel, I said unto Peter before them all, If thou, being a Jew, livest after the manner of Gentiles, and not as do the Jews, why compellest thou the Gentiles to live as do the Jews?
Rom 14:5
One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.
Rom 14:4
Who art thou that judgest another man's servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth. Yea, he shall be holden up: for God is able to make him stand.
For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things;
corruption_summary: The first Cistercian house in Ireland, 1142: Irish monks resisting an imposed foreign uniformity, with a real case on both sides and Scripture holding the balance.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is uniformity pressed where Scripture leaves liberty. The Cistercian visitors were enforcing a rule, not a gospel, and deposing Irish abbots to install foreigners is the behaviour of an empire rather than a church. The Jerusalem council's instinct was the opposite: “For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things” (Act 15:28) — the burden kept to what was necessary, and the rest left alone.

The honest other half is that national feeling is no warrant for anything either. Paul confronted Peter publicly when a custom was being used to divide the church, and he did it over practice rather than doctrine. The principle to recover is the hardest one in church life: “to his own master he standeth or falleth. Yea, he shall be holden up: for God is able to make him stand” (Rom 14:4) — liberty in things indifferent, firmness in things necessary, and the discernment to tell which is which.
roots_summary: Latin mellis fons, fountain of honey; Greek adiaphora, things indifferent; Greek anagkaios (G316), necessary; Greek eleutheria (G1657), liberty; Greek ethos (G1485), a custom.
roots_lines: Latin mellis fons — the fountain of honey; a name of promise for a first foundation.
Greek anagkaios (G316) — necessary; “no greater burden than these necessary things” (Act 15:28).
Greek eleutheria (G1657) — liberty, freedom; the New Testament's standing in things indifferent.
Greek ethos (G1485) — a custom, usage; what the Irish houses kept and the visitors came to abolish.
Greek plerophoreo (G4135) — to be fully persuaded; “Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind” (Rom 14:5).
usage: “For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us” (Act 15:28) — a council keeping the burden light.
“why compellest thou the Gentiles to live as do the Jews?” (Gal 2:14) — when a custom must be resisted.
“Who art thou that judgest another man's servant?” (Rom 14:4) — when it must be left alone.
